newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE-Pensions are new bait hooking Singapore executives.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Pensions are new bait hooking Singapore executives.

text.p: Pension plans could be the key to securing long-term corporate loyalty in Singapore's fickle executive jobs market, analysts said.
"Pension plans will be increasingly used as a retention device (for executives)," predicted Leon Potgieter, managing partner for Asia at employee benefits consultant Towers Perrin.
He told Reuters employers were desperate to retain staff as cost-effectively as possible and insurance-based products would provide the solutions.
This was because changing demographics and an aging population had forced executives to rethink their financial futures, Potgieter said.

Singapore's aged community is among the fastest growing in the world and researchers predict it could double within 20 years. Projections show that by 2030, 2.2 workers will be supporting one retired person, compared with 7.5 to one in 1990.
PRIVATE PENSIONS SEEN SOARING
The private pensions market is set to take off in Singapore due to a three-stage reform of investment rules in the country's Central Provident Fund state pension scheme.
Insurers expect about Singapore $3.0 billion (US$2.1 billion) will be pumped into private pensions over the next three years as a result.
Industry sources estimate about S$1.0 billion is currently invested in corporate plans, with significant scope to add to the existing 100 or so schemes on the island.
"The growth in the number of funds will be pretty strong, certainly up 50 percent in the next year or so," Potgieter said.
But pensions are not the only area of interest.
NEED FOR PARENTAL BENEFITS
Parental benefit policies could come on stream providing financial assistance packages for employees with dependent parents, similar to schemes which exist for dependent children.
A survey by Singapore's Ministry of Community Development showed that only 13 percent of the elderly have a financial plan for old age. Most say their children will provide for them.

"Given what's going to happen here (with changing demographics), there's going to be a need for something like that," Potgieter said, adding that Towers Perrin had already identified demand after conducting recent surveys among clients.
"People are going to look more and more to their employers to provide for their healthcare needs and they will differentiate employers on that basis," he said.
Booming Singapore's human resources bottleneck has forced employers to change pay and benefits strategies to retain executives in one of the world's most liquid employment markets.

Salary has traditionally been the arbiter of good career moves in Singapore with associated benefits seen as peripheral when a 20 percent pay increase is the carrot dangled before sought-after executives.
But with estimates pegging wage inflation well above consumer prices, employers need new retention tools.
PAY PACKAGES LIKELY TO BECOME MORE FLEXIBLE

Retirement plans, healthcare, dependency packages and other devices are now under scrutiny, as are interchangeable plans to allow executives to trade-off benefits for others, such as giving up a car for extra pension rights, said one analyst.
"I'm seeing a definite trend away from fixed to more variable pay packages," Na Boon Chong, principal consultant in Singapore at Hay Management Consultants, told Reuters.

The demand for innovation in flexible remuneration stems from the sheer number of career opportunities available in Singapore, which has virtually no unemployment and a steady stream of top flight companies setting up operations, said Na.
A December survey by Hay showed 15 percent of Singapore's professional and top management posts changed hands in 1996.
"Employee turnover is high, even for this region," said Na, pointing to executives with regional experience as particularly hot employment property.
The survey also showed average management salaries rising above six percent in 1996 compared to 1995 -- twice the rate of inflation -- despite a general economic slowdown.
"Employers are very concerned about the high levels of salaries and interest is being raised in benefits," said Na.
